title: Cozy Stories to Fall Asleep To 🌙 8 Calm Tales | Snortlo
intro:
Hello, and welcome to Snortlo. Tonight there are eight cozy stories waiting for you, each one small and calm, and read very slowly, with nothing at all to worry about.

Settle into your pillow. Let your shoulders drop a little, pull the covers up, and dim the lights, if they're still on.

There's no need to stay awake until the end. If you drift away during the first story, or the fourth, that's exactly as it should be. The stories will carry on softly without you.

Now, one long, slow breath. In, and out.

Let's begin.

stories.title: The Weather Station
stories.text:
High on a mountain, above the last of the pine trees, there was a small stone hut with a round tin roof and a tall white mast beside it. On top of the mast, three little metal cups spun in the wind, and beneath them a painted arrow swung slowly to show which way the air was moving. This was the weather station, and on most nights of the year, a woman called Ruth lived there with a woodstove, a shelf of books, and a very large logbook with a green cloth cover.

Ruth had been reading the weather on the mountain for many winters. She liked the work because it asked her to notice things, and noticing things was what she was best at. She noticed when the clouds came up the valley in the afternoon like slow sheep. She noticed when the air smelled of snow, which was a clean, thin smell, a little like a cold coin. She noticed that the stove always ticked twice before it settled, as if clearing its throat.

Every evening, at the same hour, she went out to read the instruments. Tonight the sky had cleared after a day of soft cloud, and the stars were very bright, the way they only are when you are high up and there are no town lights anywhere near. Ruth put on her thick wool hat, and her long coat, and the mittens with the fingertips that folded back. Then she took the torch from its hook by the door, and the pencil from behind her ear, and she stepped outside.

The cold met her gently. It was not a biting cold tonight, more of a still one, the kind that makes your breath hang in front of you like a small cloud of its own. The snow on the path squeaked under her boots. Squeak, squeak, squeak. Somewhere far below, a single light was showing in a farmhouse window, and Ruth gave it a little nod, the way she always did.

The first instrument lived in a white wooden box on legs, with slatted sides so the air could pass through. Ruth called it the beehive, though no bees had ever lived in it. She opened the little door and shone her torch inside. There were two thermometers, standing side by side like a pair of polite, thin gentlemen. She read the first one, and then the second, and then she read them both again, because that was the rule, and because she liked the rule.

Four degrees below freezing, she said out loud, to nobody in particular. And very calm about it.

She wrote the reading in her notebook, a little wobbly because of the mittens, but perfectly clear.

Next came the rain gauge, a short metal cylinder standing in a clear patch of snow. Tonight it held nothing but a thin ring of frost around its rim, and Ruth wrote that down too. Nothing in the gauge, she wrote. Frost on the edge, very pretty.

The office in the city probably did not need to know that the frost was pretty. But once, long ago, someone there had written back, thank you for the note about the pretty frost, and Ruth still kept that letter in a drawer.

Then she walked to the foot of the tall white mast and tipped her head back. The three little cups were turning very slowly, round and round, hardly more than a lazy spin. The painted arrow pointed to the north, then thought better of it and drifted a little to the west.

A light breeze from the northwest, said Ruth. Barely awake.

At the bottom of the mast, a small brown bird had tucked itself into a gap where the metal met the stone, and it opened one eye at the torchlight and then shut it again, very firmly. Ruth turned the torch away at once.

Sorry, she whispered. Go back to sleep.

The bird, which was round and fluffed up against the cold, did exactly that.

The last instrument was inside the hut, on the wall beside the window. It was the barometer, an old brass dial with a long black needle. Ruth went back inside, stamped the snow off her boots on the mat, and hung the torch on its hook. The warmth of the hut wrapped around her like a blanket that had been waiting by the fire.

She tapped the glass of the barometer gently with one fingernail. Tap, tap. The black needle shivered and moved a tiny bit to the right. Ruth smiled. That meant the high, settled air was staying where it was. More clear sky. More stars. A quiet night, and very likely a quiet morning too.

She sat down at the wooden table by the stove and opened the big green logbook. She copied the readings from her notebook into the log, one by one, in neat columns. Temperature. Rain. Wind. Pressure. Cloud, none. Visibility, very good. Then, in the space at the end of the row, where there was room for remarks, she wrote, one small bird asleep at the foot of the mast. Did not wish to be counted.

Then it was time for the radio. On the shelf above the table there was a grey radio set with a heavy black handset, and every evening Ruth read her figures to a man called Walt in an office down in the valley, who wrote them on a big chart with the figures from other mountains. She had never met Walt, but she knew his voice very well. It was slow and kind and always sounded as if it had a cup of tea beside it.

She lifted the handset and pressed the button.

Evening, Walt. Mountain station here.

Evening, Ruth, said the radio, with a little crackle. Go ahead when you're ready.

She read him the figures, slowly, one at a time, so there could be no mistakes. Walt read them back to her, and they matched, as they nearly always did.

Lovely, said Walt. Anything else up there tonight?

Stars, said Ruth. Rather a lot of them.

They said good night, and the radio gave one last soft crackle and went quiet.

Ruth filled the kettle from the big jug of water and set it on the stove. While it heated, she fed the stove two more logs, and it ticked twice, and settled. She made a cup of tea with a spoonful of honey in it and carried it to the window.

Outside, the mountain was white and blue under the starlight. The farmhouse light far below had gone out now. The three little cups on the mast had almost stopped, turning once, and then again a long while later, as if they were dreaming about the wind rather than feeling it.

Ruth drank her tea slowly, then rinsed the cup and set it upside down to dry. She wound the little clock on the shelf, because tomorrow she would read the instruments again at the very same hour, and the evening after that, and so on, all through the winter.

Then she climbed into the narrow bed under the window, pulled the quilt up to her chin, and switched off the lamp. The stove glowed orange behind its little glass door. The barometer needle held steady on the wall.

And outside, under all those stars, the little brown bird slept on at the foot of the mast, and the cups turned once more, very slowly, and then were still.

stories.title: Closing the Beach Hut
stories.text:
At the far end of a long pebbly beach, past the last of the fishing boats and the little wooden café with its shutters already down, there was a row of beach huts. There were twelve of them, all in a line, all painted a different colour. One was pale yellow, one was mint green, one was the blue of a summer sky, and one, the one at the very end, was a deep, cheerful red with a white door.

That was Henry's hut.

Henry had looked after the red hut for more summers than he could easily count. He had painted it himself every spring, with a brush that was now so old it had more character than bristles. And every year, on the first properly cold afternoon of the autumn, he came down to the beach to close it up for the winter.

Today was that day. He could tell as soon as he opened his front door in the morning. The air had a sharpness to it, the sea had turned from blue to a soft steel grey, and the gulls were sitting all together on the sea wall with their feathers puffed up, like a row of grumpy cushions.

Henry walked down to the beach after lunch with a canvas bag over his shoulder. In the bag were a flask of tomato soup, a tin of biscuits, a roll of string, a small screwdriver, an old towel, and a padlock he had oiled the night before so that it would close sweetly. He wore his thick blue jumper and his woolly hat, and he walked slowly, because the pebbles shifted under his feet, and because there was no rush at all.

The beach was nearly empty. A woman in a long coat was throwing a ball for a dog near the water, and the dog was bringing it back every single time with the expression of someone doing a very important job. Henry waved, and the woman waved back. The dog did not wave, because it was busy.

When he reached the red hut, Henry put down his bag and stood for a moment just looking at it. The paint was a little faded on the side that faced the sea, and there was a fine line of salt along the bottom of the door. He made a note of that in his head. Next spring, that side would get an extra coat.

He unlocked the door and swung it open. Inside, the hut smelled of warm wood and sun cream and, very faintly, of summer. There was a narrow shelf with a little stove and two mugs on it, a small folding table, a striped rug on the floor, and, stacked against the back wall, the deckchairs.

There were four of them, with wooden frames and canvas seats in faded stripes. One had red and white stripes, one green and white, one blue and white, and one, which nobody could quite explain, had orange and purple stripes. Henry's grandchildren had always argued over that one, very politely, by pretending not to want it.

Henry carried the deckchairs out one at a time and set them up on the pebbles in a row, facing the sea. Then he sat in each one, just for a moment, because it seemed only fair to say goodbye properly. The red one creaked. The green one sighed. The blue one was perfectly comfortable and always had been. The orange and purple one tipped him back a little further than he expected, and he laughed out loud, all by himself, on the empty beach.

After that, he got to work. He wiped each frame with the old towel to take off the salt and the sand. He checked the canvas for small tears and found only one, on the blue chair, which he would mend at home over the winter. He tightened a loose screw on the red one. Then he folded each chair flat, with a soft wooden clack, and leaned them together in a neat stack.

Clack. Clack. Clack. Clack.

The light was beginning to change now. The sun had come out low beneath the edge of the clouds, and it laid a long golden path across the grey water, all the way from the far horizon to the shore. The dog and the woman had gone home. The gulls on the sea wall had their eyes closed.

Henry poured himself a cup of soup from the flask and sat on the step of the hut to drink it. It was hot and thick and tasted of tomatoes and pepper, and it warmed him right down to his toes. He ate two biscuits with it, the plain kind, the kind that are better dipped. He watched the waves come in, each one turning over at the top in a curl of white foam and sliding up the pebbles with a long, slow hush, and then drawing back again with a rattle. Hush, and rattle. Hush, and rattle.

When the soup was gone, he went back inside. He rolled up the striped rug and tied it with string. He wrapped the two mugs in a tea towel and set them on the shelf. He folded the little table and leaned it in the corner. Then he carried the deckchairs in, one by one, and stood them against the back wall where they belonged, with the rolled rug laid across the top of them like a blanket over a row of sleepy children.

He looked around. Everything was tidy. Everything was in its place. On the inside of the door hung a small chalkboard that his granddaughter had put up years ago, and on it, in her round handwriting, it still said, see you in the summer, hut.

Henry did not rub it out. He never did.

He stepped outside and closed the white door behind him, slid the bolt across, and clicked the padlock shut. It closed sweetly, just as he had hoped. He laid his hand flat against the red wood for a moment, the way you might rest your hand on the neck of a friendly horse.

Sleep well, he said. Not long now.

That was not quite true. It would be a long winter, with grey mornings and frost on the sea wall. But it was the kind of thing you say, and the hut did not seem to mind.

Henry picked up his canvas bag, which was a good deal lighter now, and began to walk back along the beach. The golden path on the water was fading to pink. One by one, the lights were coming on in the houses along the seafront, small and yellow and warm.

At the top of the steps, he turned and looked back. The row of beach huts stood along the shore in the dusk, yellow and green and blue and all the rest, and at the very end, the red one, closed and quiet and waiting.

The waves came in, and went out. Hush, and rattle. Hush, and rattle.

And Henry went home for his tea.

stories.title: The Wreath Maker
stories.text:
On a narrow street in a small market town, between a bakery and a shop that sold wool, there was a florist's shop with a green front and a bell over the door. The shop was called Mabel's, because it belonged to Mabel, and Mabel had never seen any reason to call it anything else.

Tomorrow was the first frost market. Every year, when the cold finally came, the town square filled with wooden stalls and strings of little lights, and people came from all the villages around to buy honey and woolly socks and hot apple juice in paper cups. And every year, Mabel had a stall right in the middle, under the old oak tree, piled high with wreaths.

So tonight, she was making wreaths.

She had turned the sign on the door to say closed, pulled down the blind, and switched off the big lights, so that only the lamp over the workbench was on. It made a warm yellow circle on the table, and everything outside that circle went soft and shadowy, the buckets of flowers and the shelves of pots and the old clock on the wall, ticking quietly to itself.

On the workbench, Mabel had laid out everything she needed. There was a stack of round wire frames, each as wide as a dinner plate. There were great armfuls of fir branches, dark green and smelling like a forest after rain. There was a basket of pine cones, some big and some tiny, and a bowl of dried orange slices that glowed like little stained glass windows when she held them up to the lamp. There were sprigs of holly with shiny leaves, bunches of soft grey eucalyptus, a spool of brown string, and a box of ribbons in every colour you could think of.

Mabel put the kettle on in the back room, and while it boiled, she tied on her apron. It was a heavy canvas apron with a big front pocket, and in the pocket she kept her snips, a small curved knife, and a pencil that she never seemed to use but always liked to have. She made herself a mug of tea, strong, with a little milk, and set it on the corner of the bench where she would not knock it over. She had knocked it over many times before, so she knew exactly which corner was safest.

Then she began.

She took the first wire frame and a handful of fir. She snipped the branches into short pieces, each about as long as her hand, and gathered three or four of them together into a little bunch. She laid the bunch on the frame and wound the string around it, tight, twice. Then another bunch, overlapping the first, so the cut ends were hidden. Then another, and another, all the way around, like the feathers on a bird's wing.

Snip, snip. Wind, wind. Snip, snip. Wind, wind.

It was quiet, careful work, and her hands knew it so well that her mind could wander a little while she did it. She thought about the market tomorrow, and the smell of the hot apple juice, and the man at the honey stall who always gave her a spoonful to try, even though she always bought a jar anyway. She thought about the little girl who had come to her stall last year with her grandmother, and had chosen the smallest wreath on the table, and had carried it home very carefully in both arms, like a sleeping cat.

When the green ring was finished, she tied off the string and held it up. It was round and full and even. She turned it slowly in the lamplight, and it smelled wonderful.

Now came the part Mabel liked best. She tucked in three pine cones, one big and two small, at the bottom of the wreath. She wired four orange slices in a little curve along one side. She added a few sprigs of holly and two silvery stems of eucalyptus, and then she stepped back and looked at it with her head on one side.

Hmm, she said.

It needed something. She looked in the ribbon box and took out a ribbon the colour of plums, wide and soft, and tied it in a bow at the top. Then she looked again.

There, she said. That's you.

She hung the wreath on one of the hooks along the wall, and it swung gently and then was still.

The clock ticked. Outside, the street was very quiet. Now and then footsteps passed on the cobbles and faded away. The bakery next door had closed hours ago, but a faint warm smell of bread still seemed to hang in the air, the way it always did.

Mabel made another wreath, and then another. One had white ribbon and tiny pine cones. One had no ribbon at all, just holly and orange and a little bundle of cinnamon sticks tied with string, which made the whole shop smell like a kitchen at the start of winter. One was very small, about the size of a saucer, with a single red berry on it, and she smiled when she hung it up, because she was thinking of the little girl.

Her tea went cold, as it always did. She drank it anyway, because she was used to that too.

By the time the clock on the wall said half past ten, there was a whole row of wreaths along the hooks, a long green line of them, dark and full and dotted with orange and red and gold. The workbench was covered in little bits of fir and snipped string and stray needles. Mabel's fingers were sticky with sap and smelled of pine, and would go on smelling of pine all through tomorrow.

She counted the wreaths. Then she counted them again, just to be sure. There were enough.

She swept the bench clear with the side of her hand and brushed the needles into the bin. She swept the floor with the soft broom. She washed her mug and her hands in the little sink in the back room, with plenty of soap, and dried them on the towel by the door.

Then she came back into the shop and stood for a moment in the warm circle of lamplight, looking at the wreaths. They seemed to be looking back at her, in a pleased, green sort of way, as if they knew they were going somewhere tomorrow.

Through the gap at the side of the blind, Mabel could see the window of the house across the street. Frost was beginning to form on the glass in thin white feathers, starting at the corners and creeping slowly towards the middle. The first frost. Right on time.

Good, she said softly. That's everybody ready, then.

She untied her apron and hung it on its peg. She put on her coat and her scarf. She took one last look around the shop, at the buckets, and the shelves, and the long green row of wreaths in the shadows.

Then she reached up and switched off the lamp over the workbench. The warm circle went out. The shop was dark and quiet, and full of the smell of the forest.

The bell over the door gave one small, sleepy ring as she went out, and the clock on the wall went on ticking, all by itself, until morning.

stories.title: The Dog Who Counted Twice
stories.text:
On a hill farm at the end of a long, winding lane, where the stone walls ran up and down the fields like grey pencil lines, there lived a sheepdog called Bess.

Bess was black and white, with one ear that stood up and one ear that folded over, as if it had decided halfway through to have a rest. She had a white tip on her tail and a white stripe down her nose, and she had very serious brown eyes. She was not serious all the time. She liked rolling in the long grass, and the crust of the farmer's toast, and having her chest scratched in a particular spot that only the farmer could find. But when it came to the sheep, Bess was very serious indeed.

The farmer was called Tom. He was a tall, quiet man with a flat cap, a long coat, and a crook of hazel wood that his own father had carved. Tom did not say much, but Bess understood all of it anyway, and most of what he did not say as well.

Every evening, at the end of the day, Bess brought the sheep down from the top field into the yard by the barn, where they would spend the night sheltered and snug. And every evening, once they were in, she counted them.

Then she counted them again.

Nobody had taught her to do this. Tom counted the sheep too, leaning on the gate, but only ever once. Bess counted twice, every single night, and she would not settle until both counts came out the same.

Tonight was a still, chilly evening at the very end of autumn. The sky was the colour of a pigeon's wing, and the last of the light lay low across the hills. The air smelled of damp leaves and woodsmoke from the farmhouse chimney. Tom came out of the kitchen door, pulling on his coat, and whistled once, low and soft.

Bess was off before the whistle had finished. She went through the gap in the wall and up the hill at a long, easy run, keeping wide, swinging out in a big curve so as not to startle anyone. The sheep were scattered all over the top field, grazing, their woolly backs pale in the dusk, like a field of clouds that had come down to rest.

Bess slowed to a walk. She dropped low, her belly close to the grass, and moved in quietly, one careful step at a time. The nearest sheep lifted their heads and looked at her, chewing. Bess looked back. That was usually all it took. One by one, the sheep began to drift together and turn towards the gate, the way water starts to run downhill.

There was one sheep, there was always one sheep, who did not want to go. Her name, as far as Bess was concerned, was Dandelion, because she was always the last to leave the dandelions. Dandelion was a round, thoughtful ewe who believed there was always one more good mouthful of grass just a little further on. Tonight she had found a fine patch by the wall, and was not interested in the evening at all.

Bess went and stood in front of her. Not close. Just there. Just looking.

Dandelion chewed. Bess looked. Dandelion chewed a little more slowly. Bess went on looking, very patiently, with her folded ear and her serious eyes.

At last Dandelion gave a long sigh through her nose, the kind of sigh that means, oh, very well, and turned and ambled after the others.

Down the hill they went, the whole woolly crowd of them, bleating softly, with Bess weaving gently back and forth behind. Tom was waiting at the bottom with the gate swung open, and the sheep poured through it into the yard, and Tom swung the gate shut behind them and dropped the latch with a clank.

Good girl, said Tom.

Bess wagged her tail once. Then she got to work.

She trotted along the wall of the yard, looking at each sheep in turn. Not looking at them as a crowd, but one at a time, as if she were saying hello. There was the old ewe with the black face. There were the twins, who always stood together. There was the big ram with the curly horns, who was in charge of nothing but liked to think otherwise. There was the ewe who coughed politely, and the young one who was still a little nervous of everything, even the moon.

Bess did not count in numbers, not exactly. But she knew every face, and she knew how many faces there should be, and she knew how it felt when the yard was full in exactly the right way, like a jigsaw puzzle with every piece in.

She went all the way round. It felt right. Everyone was there.

Then she went all the way round again.

Tom leaned on the gate and watched her, with his cap pushed back a little. He had watched her do this every night for years, and he never tired of it. Perhaps, he thought, she simply liked saying good night to everybody twice.

Halfway through the second count, Bess stopped. She stood very still, looking at the corner by the water trough.

Dandelion was not there.

Bess's ears went up, both of them, even the folded one. Then she saw her. Dandelion had not gone anywhere at all. She had simply lain down in the deep straw behind the hay rack, where it was warm, and tucked her legs underneath her, and she was already half asleep, with her chin resting on the straw.

Bess walked over, quietly, and looked at her. Dandelion opened one eye and looked back, as if to say, what? I'm here, aren't I?

Bess's tail moved slowly from side to side. That was everybody.

She finished the second count, all the way round to the gate, and it came out the same as the first. And then, at last, she let out a long breath and sat down, right by Tom's boots.

Tom reached down and found the spot on her chest, the particular spot, and scratched it. Bess leaned against his leg and closed her eyes.

All in? said Tom.

Bess thumped her tail on the ground. All in.

The sheep were settling now. One by one, they folded down into the straw, with small grunts and sighs. The twins lay down side by side. The old ewe with the black face closed her eyes. The young nervous one looked at the moon, which was just coming up over the hill, round and pale, and decided that perhaps it was not so worrying after all, and lay down too.

Tom and Bess walked back across the yard to the farmhouse. The kitchen window was glowing gold, and when Tom opened the door, warm air rolled out to meet them, smelling of stew and the stove.

Bess went straight to her basket by the range. It was an old basket with a tartan blanket in it, and she turned around in it three times, the way dogs do, and then curled up with her nose tucked into the white tip of her tail.

Tom sat in his chair with his supper on his knees, and the fire crackled softly in the range.

And Bess, warm in her basket, with her folded ear and her serious eyes now closed, gave one small, contented sigh, because everyone was in, and she had counted, twice.

stories.title: The Orange House
stories.text:
Behind a big old house on the edge of a quiet village, at the end of a gravel path lined with low hedges, there was a long glass building with a sloping roof and a little iron chimney at one end. It was called the orange house, and it had been called that for so long that nobody remembered who had named it.

Inside, all year round, there were orange trees.

They grew in big round clay pots, standing in two long rows on either side of a brick path. Some were tall and leafy and reached nearly to the glass roof. Some were small and young and only as high as your knee. And at this time of year, in the deep of winter, almost all of them had fruit, round and bright, glowing among the dark green leaves like little lamps that someone had forgotten to switch off.

The gardener who looked after them was called Arthur. He was a small, quiet man with white hair and a soft grey cardigan with leather patches on the elbows. He had looked after the orange trees since he was a young man, when old Mr. Pell had been the gardener and Arthur had only been allowed to carry the watering can. Now Mr. Pell was long retired, living by the sea and sending Arthur postcards about the weather, and Arthur was the one who knew every tree by heart.

On this particular afternoon, the sky had gone heavy and white, and the air had that quiet, padded feeling that comes before snow. The voice on the radio at lunchtime had said there would be a hard frost tonight, the hardest of the winter so far. So Arthur put on his boots and his scarf and went down to the orange house with a wheelbarrow full of straw.

When he opened the door, the warmth inside came out to greet him, and with it the smell. It was a smell like nothing else, green and sweet and sharp all at once, the smell of orange leaves and damp earth and warm brick. Arthur stood in the doorway and breathed it in, as he always did, before he stepped inside and shut the door behind him.

At the far end of the orange house, the little iron stove was already burning. Arthur had lit it that morning and fed it at lunchtime, and now he opened its door and fed it again, with three good logs from the basket. The fire caught and roared softly, and Arthur closed the door, and the stove began to tick and hum.

The stove would keep the air warm enough through the night. But the pots were a different matter. On the coldest nights, a chill could creep up through the brick floor and into the clay, and get at the roots, and the roots of orange trees do not like the cold at all. So every winter, on the night of the first hard frost, Arthur wrapped the pots in straw.

He started at the end nearest the stove, with the oldest tree of all. It had a thick, twisted trunk and a wide, round crown of leaves, and its oranges were small and very dark, almost red. Arthur called it the grandmother.

Good afternoon, he said to it. Bit of a cold one coming.

He took a big armful of straw from the wheelbarrow and packed it around the base of the pot, all the way round, thick and loose and golden. Then he took a length of old sacking and wrapped it around the straw, and tied it with garden twine, not too tight, just snug. When he was done, the grandmother looked as if she were wearing a fat woolly skirt.

There you are, said Arthur. Warm as toast.

He moved on to the next tree, and the next. Each one got its armful of straw, its sacking, and its twine. Arthur worked slowly and carefully, the way he did everything. Now and then he stopped to turn a leaf over, or to touch an orange gently to see if it was ready.

Outside, the light was going. The white sky turned grey, and then a soft dark blue. And then, while Arthur was halfway down the second row, the first snowflake drifted down and settled on the glass roof just above his head.

He stopped and looked up at it. It was a big, soft flake, the kind that comes down slowly, turning as it falls. Then there was another, and another, and soon the whole sky above the orange house was full of them, falling silently through the dark and settling on the glass in a thin white layer.

Inside, it was warm and green and golden. Outside, it was snowing. Arthur thought, as he always did at moments like this, that he must have the nicest job in the whole world.

He finished the second row. The very last pot held the smallest tree, a young one he had grown himself from a cutting three summers ago. It had only a handful of leaves and only one orange, a small green one that had not yet made up its mind to ripen. Arthur knelt down beside it, with a little creak of the knees, and wrapped its pot with extra care, using twice as much straw as it really needed.

Just to be on the safe side, he told it.

When all the pots were wrapped, Arthur pushed the empty wheelbarrow back to the door and swept the loose straw off the brick path with a soft broom. Then he took the watering can and gave each tree a small drink, just enough to keep the soil from drying out near the stove. The water made a gentle trickling sound as it soaked into the earth.

Last of all, he went back to the grandmother tree and chose an orange. It came away from the branch with a little twist and a soft snap, and it sat in his palm, cool and heavy and smooth.

He sat down on the low wooden bench beside the stove and peeled the orange slowly, in one long curling strip, the way his mother had taught him. The smell filled the air, bright and sharp and sweet. He ate it piece by piece, looking out through the glass at the snow, which was falling thicker now, softly covering the gravel path and the hedges and the roof of the big old house.

When the orange was finished, he laid the peel on top of the stove, where it would warm and curl and make the whole orange house smell even more of oranges, all through the night.

Then he stood up, checked the stove one last time, and turned down the little damper so it would burn slowly until morning. He looked along the two long rows of trees, each one tucked up in its straw, each one with its small lamps of fruit glowing in the dim light.

Good night, all, he said quietly.

He opened the door and stepped out into the snow, and closed it gently behind him. As he crunched back up the path towards the house, he turned once to look back. The orange house sat at the bottom of the garden, its glass roof white with snow, and inside, faint and warm and golden, the little stove glowed among the sleeping trees.

stories.title: The Skating Pond
stories.text:
In the middle of a small town, at the bottom of a sloping park, there was a pond. In summer it was full of ducks and lily pads, and children floated paper boats on it, and old men sat on the benches around it with newspapers they did not really read. But in the very coldest part of winter, the pond froze over, thick and smooth and grey, and then it became the skating pond.

The person who looked after the skating pond was called June.

June had a little wooden hut at the edge of the ice, with a stove inside, and a counter where she lent out skates, and a big kettle that was always on. Around the pond, strung from tree to tree, there were long strings of round white lights, and every evening at dusk June switched them on, and the whole pond glowed like the inside of a shell.

This evening, the skating had been busy. There had been families wobbling along holding hands, and teenagers going round and round very fast and pretending not to be cold, and a very old couple who skated slowly, arm in arm, as if they were dancing to music nobody else could hear. There had been one small boy in a red hat who sat down on the ice many times and laughed every single time, and got up again, and sat down again, and went home with his cheeks pink and his eyes shining.

Now it was late, and the skaters had all gone home. The last of them had handed back their skates at the counter and said thank you and good night, and walked away up the path through the park, their voices fading among the trees. June had wiped down the skates and hung them on their pegs by size, from the tiniest to the biggest, in a long neat row.

And now it was time to smooth the ice.

June put on her warm coat, her thick gloves, and her hat with the bobble on top. She wheeled out the scraper from the back of the hut. It was a wide, flat metal blade on the end of a long handle, a bit like an enormous snow shovel, and it was painted green, and it was older than June was.

She stepped out onto the ice. Under the strings of lights, the surface was scratched and scuffed all over, with long curving lines where the skaters had gone round and round, and little rough patches where the small boy in the red hat had sat down.

June set the blade down at one edge of the pond and began to push.

Shh, said the scraper, as it slid across the ice. Shh.

It shaved off a thin layer of frost and scratches, and left behind it a wide, clean stripe, darker and smoother than the ice around it. At the far side of the pond, June turned around and came back, with the next stripe just beside the first. Shh. And back again. Shh.

It was slow work, and she did not hurry it. Up and back, up and back, stripe by stripe, all the way across the pond. The lights swayed very gently on their strings above her, and their reflections swayed with them in the ice. Her breath made small clouds that floated up and vanished.

The park was very quiet now. Beyond the trees, the town was settling down for the night, and somewhere a dog barked once and then thought better of it. Overhead, the sky was clear and black, and the stars were out, small and sharp and cold.

Halfway across the pond, June stopped to rest. She leaned on the handle of the scraper and looked around. On one of the benches at the edge of the ice, a fat grey pigeon was sitting all puffed up, like a little feathered teapot. It looked at June, and June looked at it.

You should be in bed, she told it.

The pigeon did not reply. It simply tucked its head a little further into its feathers, as if to say that it was in bed, thank you, and this was its bed.

June smiled and went back to her scraping. Shh. Shh.

When the whole pond had been scraped, she wheeled the scraper back to the hut and leaned it against the wall. Then she came out again with the water cart. This was a big metal barrel on two wheels, with a long pipe across the back full of tiny holes, and a soft cloth hanging from the pipe that trailed along behind it like the train of a gown. She had filled the barrel earlier with warm water from the tap in the hut.

She opened the little valve, and the water began to trickle out through the holes, onto the cloth, and from the cloth onto the ice. June walked slowly backwards across the pond, drawing the cart along with her. Behind it, the cloth left a thin, shining film of water, which spread out and filled every last scratch and dent, and then, in the cold night air, began very quietly to freeze.

Up and back she went again, slower this time, so the water could lie perfectly flat. When she reached the edge for the last time, she closed the valve, turned round, and looked.

The whole pond was like glass. Like a mirror. The strings of lights were reflected in it so clearly that there seemed to be two sets of lights, one above and one below, and the stars too, all of them, lying on the ice as if they had come down for a rest.

June stood very still and looked at it for a long time. She did this every night, and it never stopped being lovely.

Then she went back into the hut, where the stove was warm and the kettle was singing. She made a cup of hot chocolate, thick and sweet, and sat on the stool by the window to drink it. Through the glass, she could see the pond, smooth and shining under the lights. The pigeon was still on its bench, a small grey shape, fast asleep.

Tomorrow, the skaters would come back. The families and the teenagers and the old couple who danced, and perhaps the small boy in the red hat, ready to sit down on the ice again and laugh. And they would find it waiting for them, smooth and new, as if nobody had ever skated on it before.

June finished her chocolate and washed the cup. She checked that all the skates were hanging in their right places. She banked down the stove so the hut would stay warm until morning. Then she put on her coat and her hat with the bobble, stepped outside, and locked the door behind her.

Last of all, she reached up to the switch on the side of the hut and turned off the lights.

All along the strings, the round white bulbs went dark together, and their reflections in the ice went dark with them. And then there was only the pond, silver and still under the stars, and the pigeon asleep on its bench, and June's footsteps going softly away up the path, crunch, crunch, crunch, into the quiet of the night.

stories.title: The Quiet Bell Ringer
stories.text:
In a small village tucked into a fold of the hills, there was a green, and in the middle of the green there stood an old stone tower. Nobody was quite sure why it had been built. Some people said it had once been part of a market hall, and some said it had simply been built because someone, long ago, thought a village ought to have a tower. But everyone agreed on one thing. It had the loveliest bells for miles around.

There were six of them, hanging in a wooden frame at the very top of the tower. They ranged from a little high bell with a voice like a teaspoon tapped against a glass, to a great deep bell whose note you could feel in your chest. On holidays and on summer evenings, a team of ringers climbed the tower and pulled the long ropes, and the bells rang out across the green and over the rooftops and up into the hills.

Theo was one of the ringers. He was the youngest of them, though he was not especially young, and he was the newest, though he had been ringing for almost two years. He was a tall, gentle man who worked in the bookshop on the corner, and he had big careful hands, and he was still, if he was honest, a little bit in awe of the bells.

There was a big ring coming up, for the midwinter fair at the end of the month, and Theo had been given a new pattern to learn. It was a long, winding piece, where the bells changed places with each other over and over, like dancers swapping partners, and Theo kept losing his place in the middle.

So tonight, with the others' blessing, he had come to the tower to practise on his own.

It was snowing. It had been snowing since teatime, the soft, steady, windless kind of snow that falls straight down and settles on everything. The green was white and smooth, with only Theo's own footprints crossing it, from the bookshop to the tower door. The houses around the green had snow on their roofs and snow on their windowsills, and their windows glowed yellow in the blue evening.

Theo unlocked the little arched door at the bottom of the tower and went in, stamping the snow off his boots. He switched on the light, a single bulb in a glass shade, and climbed the narrow spiral staircase, round and round, with one hand on the cool stone wall. The steps were worn in the middle, smooth and dipped, from all the feet that had climbed them before his.

At the top of the stairs was the ringing room. It was a small square room with wooden floorboards and a little window on each side, and from the ceiling hung six ropes, each with a soft woollen grip striped in red and white and blue. On the walls were old wooden boards painted with the names of ringers from long ago, and a small framed photograph of the team, all smiling, with Theo at the end looking slightly surprised.

Theo did not want to disturb the whole village, not on a snowy evening when people were settling down by their fires. So before he began, he did what the old ringers had taught him. He climbed the short ladder to the bell chamber and fitted his bell with a muffle, a thick leather pad that fastened over the clapper, so that it would ring softly, with a sound like a voice speaking very quietly in another room.

Then he came back down, took hold of the rope for the fourth bell, which was his, and took a slow breath.

He pulled.

Far above, the bell swung, and the muffled clapper struck it, and a soft round note came down through the ceiling. Dong. Not a ringing clang, but a hum, warm and low, like a cat purring on the other side of a door.

Theo smiled. He pulled again. Dong. And then he began to work through the pattern, slowly, counting the places in his head, pulling the rope at just the right moment and letting it rise again through his hands, the striped grip slipping up and down between his fingers.

Because he was alone, he could only ring his own bell. But he knew the pattern was about when, not about how many. So he rang his bell in its right places, and in the gaps he hummed the other bells under his breath, very quietly, so he would know where he was. Dong, hum, hum, dong, hum, hum, hum, dong.

He lost his place in the middle, as he always did. He stopped, let the rope settle, and started again from the beginning. He lost it again, a little later this time. He stopped, and started again.

Outside, the snow fell and fell. Through the little window, he could see the green, white and empty, and the houses around it, and the glow of the street lamp by the bus shelter, with snowflakes drifting through its light like moths.

He tried a fourth time. And this time, he did not lose his place. He got through the middle, where the pattern twisted round on itself, and out the other side, and all the way to the end, where the bells came back into their starting order, like a family coming home and sitting down in their usual chairs.

Theo let the rope go still and stood there for a moment, breathing, with a big slow smile spreading across his face.

Well, he said out loud, to the empty room. Well, well.

He rang it once more, just to be sure. It went perfectly again.

In the houses around the green, people heard the soft muffled bell through the falling snow, very faint and far away, and some of them looked up from their books or their knitting. That'll be Theo, they thought, practising. And they went back to their books and their knitting, and the soft dong, dong of the bell seemed to fit somehow with the snow, and the fire, and the quiet.

When he was finished, Theo climbed the ladder again, took off the muffle, and laid it neatly in its wooden box. He came down and tied up the rope, looping it carefully and tucking the striped grip into the loop, so that all six ropes hung tidy and still. He switched off the light in the ringing room and went down the spiral stairs, round and round, in the glow of the bulb at the bottom.

He locked the arched door behind him and stepped out onto the green.

The snow was still falling. His footprints from earlier had already softened and filled, and the green was nearly smooth again. Theo walked slowly back across it, leaving a new line of footprints behind him, his breath making clouds in the cold air. The houses glowed. The street lamp hummed. The snow made the softest sound in the world, which is almost no sound at all.

At the bookshop door, he turned and looked back at the tower. It stood in the middle of the white green, dark and tall and quiet, with snow along every ledge and a little cap of white on its top.

And in his head, very softly, the pattern was still ringing. Dong, hum, hum, dong. All the way through, and home again, and still.

stories.title: The Map of the Quiet Valley
stories.text:
At the top of a tall, narrow house on a crooked street, up three flights of creaking stairs, there was an attic room with a slanting ceiling and a round window that looked out over the rooftops. This was the workroom of Nora, the map maker.

Nora made maps by hand. Not maps of whole countries, or cities, or the great wide seas. She made small maps of small places. A map of a garden, for a woman who wanted to remember where she had planted everything. A map of a riverside walk, for a man who took it every Sunday with his dog.

Tonight, she was finishing a map of a valley.

She had walked the valley herself, back in the autumn, over many slow days with a notebook and a pencil and a flask of tea. She had followed the stream from its beginning, a little trickle among mossy stones at the top of the hill, all the way down to where it joined the river at the bottom. She had counted the bridges. She had sketched the farmhouses and the barns and the little stone mill. She had sat on a wall and drawn the shape of the hills against the sky, and a robin had sat on the wall beside her and watched her do it, as if checking her work.

Now all those notes and sketches were spread across the big wooden table in the attic, and in the middle of them, pinned flat at each corner, was the map itself, nearly finished.

It was evening, and outside it was raining softly. Nora could hear it on the slates above her head, a gentle, steady patter, and see it running down the round window in little silver threads. She had lit three candles in brass holders and set them around the table, because she liked to do the last part of a map by candlelight. It made the paper glow warm and golden, and the ink look deep and soft, and it made the whole room feel very still and very far away from everything.

She sat on her tall stool and drew the map towards her. Then she dipped her finest pen into the bottle of brown ink, wiped it carefully on the rim, and leaned in close.

The hills were already drawn. She had done those first, weeks ago, with hundreds of tiny fine lines, close together where the slopes were steep and far apart where they were gentle, so that the hills seemed to rise softly from the paper. The stream was drawn too, a thin, wandering blue line that curled down the middle of the valley like a ribbon dropped from a window.

Tonight, she was drawing the small things.

She began with the trees. Along the banks of the stream, she drew them one at a time, each a tiny round puff with a little dot of shadow beneath it. Dot, puff. Dot, puff. Here was a clump of willows by the first bridge. Here was the old oak in the middle of the big meadow, which she drew a little larger than the others, because it deserved it. Here was the line of beech trees along the lane, drawn close together, like friends walking arm in arm.

Then the bridges. There were five of them, and she drew each one carefully, a tiny curved line over the stream, with two small dots for the stones at either end. The little wooden footbridge near the top. The stone bridge with three arches by the mill. The flat bridge made of a single slab of rock, where she had sat for a whole afternoon with her feet nearly in the water.

The candles flickered gently. The rain went on pattering on the roof. Somewhere below, in the house, a clock struck the hour, slow and muffled, and Nora counted the chimes without really meaning to, and then forgot what number she had got to.

Next came the buildings. She drew the farmhouses as little squares with tiny pointed roofs, and beside each one she wrote its name in very small, neat letters. High Barn. Brook Farm. The Old Dairy. She drew the mill beside the stream, with a tiny wheel and a curl of water beneath it. She drew the little schoolhouse on the hill, with its bell on top, and the row of cottages by the lower bridge, each one exactly the same size, like a row of sugar cubes.

She drew the paths as fine dotted lines, winding between the fields and over the stiles. She drew the stone walls as thin unbroken lines, dividing the valley into a patchwork of fields, some long and narrow, some square, and some shaped like no shape at all.

Last of all, she drew the small extra things, the things that were not really needed on a map but that she always liked to add. A tiny heron standing in the stream near the mill. A tiny sheep in one of the high fields. And on the wall by the flat stone bridge, so small you would need to look very closely to see it, a tiny robin.

She sat back and looked at it.

Then she took her softest brush and a little dish of pale watercolour, and she began to wash in the colours, very lightly. A soft green for the meadows. A darker green for the woods. A pale gold for the fields where the barley had grown. A wash of soft grey blue for the sky above the hills. The colours spread gently into the paper and dried, slowly, in the candlelight.

When the paint was dry, she picked up her pen one more time. Across the top of the map, in her best and most careful lettering, with little curls on the capitals, she wrote the name of the place. The Quiet Valley. And underneath, smaller, she wrote, drawn and walked by Nora, in the autumn.

Then she put down the pen.

Nora sat for a long time, just looking at the map. The candlelight moved softly over it, and the little trees and bridges and houses seemed almost to stir, as if the valley itself were settling down for the night. She could almost hear the stream running over its stones, and smell the wet grass, and see the robin hopping along the wall.

Outside, the rain was easing now, the patter on the slates growing softer and slower. The round window was dark and dotted with drops.

Nora cleaned her pen and put the lid on the ink. She washed her brush and laid it flat to dry. She gathered her notes and sketches into a neat pile, tied them with a ribbon, and put them in the drawer with all the others. She left the map where it was, pinned flat on the table, so the ink could rest overnight.

Then, one by one, she blew out the candles.

The first one, at the top of the valley. The second one, by the mill. And the last one, nearest the little robin on the wall.

Each one gave a small curl of grey smoke that drifted up towards the slanting ceiling and disappeared. And the attic was dark and quiet, and the map lay sleeping on the table, and outside, the very last of the rain dripped softly from the gutter, drip, and drip, and drip, until it stopped.

outro:
And that is the end of tonight's stories.

The cups on the mountain mast are still. The red beach hut is locked and waiting for summer. The wreaths are ready for the frost market. Bess has counted twice, and everyone is in. The orange trees are tucked up in straw, the skating pond lies silver, Theo's footprints are filling with snow, and the last candle is out over the quiet valley.

More gentle stories are on the channel, whenever you need them.

Good night, and sleep well.
description:
Eight cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly and softly to help you unwind and drift off.
A mountain weather station, a beach hut closing for winter, a florist's frost market wreaths, a sheepdog who counts twice, a glasshouse of winter oranges, a skating pond at night, a quiet bell ringer in the snow and a map maker by candlelight.
No drama, no cliffhangers, just calm.
Good night 🌙
